messages.content: Write a blog post announcing version 2.0 of an API client library. Around 250 words.

output:
A blog post needs a product, so I invented one. Swap the name and numbers for yours.

---

# Fetchr 2.0

Fetchr 2.0 is out. It is a rewrite, and it will break your code.

Start with the reason. The 1.x client wrapped callbacks in promises in a thin layer that everyone eventually reached past. Half the issues we closed last year were people fighting that layer. So we took it out.

**Native async, no wrapper.** Every method returns a promise. Requests are `AbortSignal`-aware, so cancelling a React effect actually cancels the socket.

**Pagination is an async iterator.** `for await (const user of client.users.list())` walks every page. No cursor bookkeeping. The old `.nextPage()` still exists in the compat build and logs a deprecation warning once per process.

**Retries you can inspect.** Retry policy is a plain object you pass in, not a constructor flag. Failed attempts show up on `err.attempts` with status, latency, and the retry-after header we obeyed.

**Types generated from the spec.** Response shapes come out of our OpenAPI document at build time. When we ship a field, you get it in the same release instead of three weeks later.

The bundle dropped from 41 kB to 12 kB gzipped, mostly by dropping the polyfills for Node 14.

Migrating: run `npx fetchr-codemod v2`. It handles the callback-to-await conversion and the renamed options. For our own dashboard it touched 340 call sites and left 6 for a human. The remaining six were all custom retry logic, which is the one thing we could not guess at.

1.x gets security patches through June 2027.
